title: Behind the Front Line
gist: CNAS report 'Behind the Front Line' argues the Department of War's nearest-term agentic-AI wins lie in support functions — supply, predictive maintenance and operational planning — rather than lethal autonomous weapons, but past automation efforts have largely failed due to siloed data, outdated policy and a 'fly to fail' culture. It recommends training, unified real-time data, senior authority to clear cross-agency roadblocks, buying commercial dual-use agentic tools via DIU, and guardrails including phased deployment, continuous monitoring and red teaming.

themes.theme: Support functions as first agentic-AI wins

insights.claim: Agentic AI is likely to affect the US military's critical enabling functions — supply, maintenance and planning — much sooner than autonomous weapon systems, and these support-side deployments will inform later AI integration into weapons.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Near-term defense-AI spending is more likely to flow to logistics, maintenance and planning software than to lethal autonomy.

insights.claim: Focusing first on support functions rather than lethal autonomous weapons both delivers benefits sooner and buys the Department of War time to work out how agentic systems fit international humanitarian law and DoDD 3000.09.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Regulatory friction is lower for back-office/enabling AI — a faster procurement path for vendors.
insights.locator: Agentic AI—which combines the AI reasoning

insights.claim: The report defines an AI agent as a system that takes a high-level goal from a user or another agent and uses reasoning and adaptation to deconstruct it into actions and execute them with minimal human intervention, noting there is no research consensus on the definition.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A working definition the Pentagon may adopt shapes what products qualify as 'agentic' in requirements.
insights.quote: An AI agent takes a high-level goal from a user or another AI agent and uses reasoning and adaptation to deconstruct the goal and execute actions to achieve it with minimal human intervention.
insights.locator: An AI agent takes a high-level goal

insights.claim: OpenAI, Google and Anthropic have invested in agentic tools around their flagship LLMs, and open-source scaffold OpenClaw drew wide attention for desktop agent uses; these commercial workflows have direct parallels to military maintenance, sustainment and planning.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Commercial frontier-AI vendors have a credible dual-use path into defense support functions.
insights.locator: Agentic AI—which combines the AI reasoning

insights.claim: Past efforts to move the Joint Force from costly human-centric processes to automation have largely failed across the defense enterprise; successes like the Navy's advanced materiel tracking remain limited in scale and have not diffused.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Expect slow, uneven adoption — temper near-term revenue expectations for defense-AI vendors.

insights.claim: Future operations require shifting from today's 'pull' supply system driven by unit orders to a 'push' system that anticipates needs and delivers semi-automatically — what the Army calls 'precision logistics'.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Demand for sensors, predictive analytics and AI logistics platforms across the services.

insights.claim: The Defense Logistics Agency handles an estimated 10 million digital invoices and orders per week, and TRANSCOM moved about 331,000 tons of cargo by air and 13.1 million square feet of cargo by sea in 2023.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Scale of the addressable data/automation problem in US military logistics.

insights.claim: The three enablers for a push supply system are real-time visibility of all supplies (e.g., Navy RFID tags in shipyards and warehouses), a unified ordering system (DLA's DAAS since the mid-1990s), and demand prediction from historical data.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: RFID/sensor and data-integration vendors are prerequisites before agentic logistics can work.

insights.claim: DEFCON AI's Artiv, demonstrated in Talisman Sabre exercises, uses mathematical optimization to recommend theater resupply plans meeting user constraints within minutes.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: An example of a startup already positioned in AI-enabled military logistics planning.

insights.claim: Existing supply common-operating-picture and order systems remain siloed and limited by manual data entry, and predictive sustainment tools are still experimental pilots across the services.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Data integration is the bottleneck — opportunities for data-fabric and integration contractors.

insights.claim: In a US-China conflict, agents could make supply a first-order planning consideration, automatically evaluating OPLAN feasibility, red-teaming plans against adversary capabilities and identifying bottlenecks to pre-emplace materiel in theater.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Contested-logistics AI is central to Indo-Pacific war readiness spending.
insights.locator: With the critical role that contested logistics

insights.claim: The report's 2030 scenario envisions a US-China war in which swarms of small UAS deplete surface ships' 20mm close-in-weapon rounds and Coyote counter-UAS missiles, with an agent producing a theater resupply plan in minutes.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Highlights counter-UAS munitions depth as a key vulnerability and procurement priority.

themes.theme: Predictive maintenance and the readiness gap

insights.claim: The Department of War spends an estimated $90 billion a year on planned and unplanned maintenance for ground, sea and air systems, yet Joint Force readiness remains persistently low.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Large spending pool where predictive-maintenance AI could claim savings — a target market for vendors.

insights.claim: Despite a Pentagon mandate since the early 2000s for Condition-Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+), it remains critically under-implemented with little demonstrable effect.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Two decades of failed mandate suggests cultural/policy barriers, not technology, govern adoption speed.

insights.claim: An entrenched 'fly to fail' culture and DLA rules requiring broken parts to be turned in before replacements are issued have obstructed predictive maintenance; pilot projects needed special dispensations to replace parts before they failed.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Policy change at DLA is a leading indicator for whether predictive-maintenance programs can scale.

insights.claim: Agentic maintenance can be modeled as five stages — sensing, detection, diagnosis, requisition and scheduling — each handled by AI agents at platform, fleet and command levels that must coordinate to deconflict repairs.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Multi-agent orchestration is the technical crux — favors vendors with integration and orchestration capabilities.
insights.locator: As a military function, maintenance is not

insights.claim: LLMs excel at analyzing the mixed structured and unstructured data in technical manuals and specifications, making root-cause diagnosis a step where agentic tools with strong reasoning will be especially beneficial.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Diagnosis is the most LLM-native maintenance use case — likely early deployment area.
insights.locator: Root cause analysis requires AI agents

insights.claim: Without access to all necessary data — including manufacturer intellectual property the GAO says is lacking — agentic maintenance tools will be no more effective than today's human-driven approach.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Technical-data rights disputes between DoD and primes will gate AI maintenance value.
insights.quote: However, without the ability to access and interrogate all the necessary data, they will not be any more effective than the current human-driven approach to maintenance.
insights.locator: The availability of the data necessary

insights.claim: Transitioning to agentic maintenance carries high up-front costs for health-monitoring sensors on new and legacy systems, retraining and data infrastructure, and AI cannot fix persistent spare-parts shortages, maintainer gaps or accumulated repair debt.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: AI is not a substitute for parts supply-chain and shipyard capacity investment.

insights.claim: Delayed maintenance causes platforms to deteriorate further and spreads backlogs, sometimes leading to premature retirement from cost overruns; shortages of qualified maintainers for systems like the B-2 Spirit illustrate the constraint.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Maintenance backlogs erode readiness and fleet size — supports demand for sustainment services.

insights.claim: In the first 100 hours of the war in Iran, the United States and Israel claimed strikes on more than 4,000 targets, showing the pace of conflict is accelerating, fueled by AI.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: High-tempo AI-enabled targeting drives munitions expenditure and demand for planning automation.

insights.claim: Planning documentation such as Time-Phased Force Deployment Data is still manually built and updated, so agentic tools can offload routine work and cut plan development from months to days.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Planning software is a sizable greenfield for defense-AI vendors.
insights.locator: Undertaking the complete pipeline of planning

insights.claim: Agentic planning tools can move commanders beyond 'satisficing' — choosing the first good-enough plan under time pressure — toward optimized courses of action by rapidly exploring alternatives.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Decision-quality gains, not just speed, are the value proposition for planning AI.

insights.claim: The 'triangle of agentic planning' links a human planner, AI agents and modeling-and-simulation tools: agents generate fast approximate candidate solutions to narrow costly M&S searches, while humans check assumptions and add novel ideas.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Value accrues to vendors that integrate LLM agents with existing simulation stacks rather than replacing them.
insights.locator: Rather than AI agents serving primarily

insights.claim: The Maven Smart System already fuses real-time sensor data for situational awareness and targeting, and LLMs on classified and unclassified networks can query doctrine and summarize intelligence; next comes producing concrete actions for review.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Existing programs of record like Maven are the beachhead for agentic upgrades.
insights.locator: The department has made some inroads

insights.claim: LLM hallucinations can misdirect military planners who are not prepared to critically evaluate AI outputs, and training-data bias can introduce faulty reasoning into plans.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Human oversight and evaluation tooling remain mandatory — slows full automation.

insights.claim: AI systems become a new attack surface for adversaries through data poisoning and adversarial examples, and databases feeding agents are themselves targets.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Creates demand for AI security, red-teaming and data-integrity products in defense.
insights.locator: Storing, cleaning, and managing this data

insights.claim: A catch-22 arises: planners must use AI to offload cognitive load while retaining manual planning skills to adjudicate AI options, a skill-atrophy problem the Pentagon has studied for autonomous weapons but neglected for support functions.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Training and professional-education redesign is a hidden cost of AI adoption.
insights.locator: Future planners will need to retain

insights.claim: Users must develop calibrated trust between overtrust and undertrust, aided by explainability features such as auditable reasoning chains, calibrated confidence scores and tool-call logs.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Explainability and audit-logging features become procurement differentiators.
insights.locator: A component of training and system design

insights.claim: The Department of War should use organizations like the Defense Innovation Unit to identify and adapt commercial dual-use agentic tools rather than relying on traditional defense-specific software acquisition.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Positive for commercial AI firms selling into defense via DIU-style fast pathways.
insights.locator: Recommendations to Enable Agentic AI Implementation

insights.claim: Agentic adoption needs high-level leadership with authority to clear cross-agency roadblocks, since policies like DLA's parts rules stymied earlier predictive-maintenance efforts.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Watch for senior-level AI adoption mandates as a catalyst for spending.
insights.locator: Recommendations to Enable Agentic AI Implementation

insights.claim: Guardrails should include phased deployment with developer-user feedback, continuous monitoring and long-term developer support, operator-level ad-hoc agent experimentation, and lifecycle testing, evaluation and red teaming — accepting that tools will never be immune to attack.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Implies recurring sustainment and T&E contracts rather than one-off software buys.
insights.quote: The solution is not to strive for tools that are immune to attacks.
